source: Hampton (1988) Overextension of conjunctive concepts: evidence for a unitary model of typicality and class inclusion (Exp 1)
finding: People put items in a conjunction (e.g. protective clothing) that they reject from the head noun category (clothing). This breaks the logical rule that a conjunction cannot be larger than its part.
numbers: Exp 1: 8 compounds from furniture, vehicles, clothing; 127 items. 93 items were more likely in the conjunction than the head category; only 22 the reverse. Mean [+ -] pattern (in compound, not in category) 26% +/-7 (compound rated first) and 22% +/-8 (category first). 66% of subjects rejected 'all garden furniture is furniture' in favour of 'some are not'.
limits: Overextension is not noise: later model with random re-responding predicted too few overextensions.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a merged concept to be a subset of its parents. A seed pair may fit the blend better than either parent.

source: Hampton (1988) Overextension of conjunctive concepts (Exp 2, sports and games)
finding: Sports-which-are-games. Items that were good in one set but poor in the other were often accepted in the conjunction. Strong fit to one concept compensates for weak fit to the other.
numbers: Chess: 61% would not call it a sport, yet 51% rated it in sports-which-are-games. Of games that were not sports, 25% still got positive conjunction ratings; of sports that were not games, 54%. Stage 1 order cells had about 8 to 9 participants each (35 total).
limits: Small cells; sports and games overlap a lot.
agent_relevance: Merging is closer to a weighted average of the parents than a minimum. Strong match on one parent can carry a weak match on the other.

source: Hampton (1988) Overextension of conjunctive concepts (error-model test)
finding: Hampton tested whether overextension could come from a contrast effect plus random subject variability. It could not.
numbers: With recall parameter u=0 the model predicted 42% [+ - +] and 24% [- + +] overextension but about twice the observed underextension. With u fitted to the underextension (mean u=.512), predicted overextension fell well below observed.
limits: Depends on the two-stage design; item-based estimates.
agent_relevance: A method the agent can copy: before trusting an odd blend result, test whether plain noise explains it.

source: Hampton (1988) Overextension of conjunctive concepts (theory: composite prototype)
finding: Proposed the composite prototype model: the two concepts' intensions (attribute sets) are merged into one composite prototype. Membership in single and combined concepts both come from similarity to a prototype above a criterion (unitary hypothesis).
numbers: No single number; the model is qualitative. Dominance of one constituent and non-commutativity (A which are B differs from B which are A) are also reported.
limits: Qualitative, not fitted; Hampton says precise quantification was not warranted given small samples.
agent_relevance: A combination step should build a new attribute list from both parents, then judge fit against that list.

source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts (chapter, 1987 study)
finding: Emergent attributes (true of the combination, of neither part) come from two routes: extensional feedback (pet birds talk, known from real instances) and scenario construction (pet birds live in cages, worked out from conflict).
numbers: 1987 study, strict scoring: 3 of 174 attributes emergent; lenient scoring: 11. Of 37 attributes unimportant to both parents, only about 8% were important to both forms of the conjunction. Emergence was higher for low-overlap pairs (pets and birds) than high-overlap pairs (sports and games, machines and vehicles).
limits: Hampton concludes there is little evidence for creative emergence in ordinary conjunctions; most emergence is looked up from the world.
agent_relevance: Most 'new' properties of a blend are retrieved, not invented. True invention needs a scenario step. Weigh this when seeding distant pairs.

source: Hampton (1987, via 1996 JEP intro) Inheritance of attributes in natural concept conjunctions: necessity and impossibility constraints
finding: Attributes necessary for one parent are always inherited by the conjunction. Attributes impossible for the other parent are impossible for the conjunction. Weaker generic attributes can fail to transfer when they conflict (warm and cuddly pets do not carry to fish which are pets).
numbers: Importance of an attribute for the conjunction is predicted by a weighted average of its importance for each parent, plus a separate effect of attribute conflict. Two kinds of noncompositional effect: attributes lost (birds migrate, pet birds do not) and attributes gained (talk, live in cages).
limits: Second-hand: the 1987 paper (Memory and Cognition 15, 55-71) would not open; read through Hampton's own summary in the 1996 JEP paper.
agent_relevance: Two hard, code-checkable rules for a combination operator: carry necessary properties; block properties the other parent forbids.

source: Hampton (1996) Emergent attributes in combined concepts: negated conjunctions and evaluative pairs
finding: With negated conjunctions (A which are not B) extensional feedback is ruled out, so remaining emergence is closer to construction. It is rare for neutral pairs but large for evaluative, antagonistic pairs.
numbers: Six category pairs: 51 attributes with median 0% for the head noun; 24 also 0% for the conjunction, 11 violated slightly, only 6 reached 10% or more (emergent). Four evaluative pairs: 210 attributes; of 65 true of the own side, 11 (17%) inherited; of 80 true of the other side, 55 (69%) inherited; of 63 false for both, 22 (35%) true of the conjunction.
limits: Rating-based; small stimulus set; evaluative pairs are special.
agent_relevance: When two ideas clash in value, the blend keeps the negative parts of the other idea more than the positive parts of its own. Watch for this bias.

source: Hampton (1996) Conjunctions of visually based categories: overextension and compensation (Exp 1)
finding: Overextension also occurs with pictures (ambiguous coloured letters H/A and cartoon faces), so it is not an artefact of vague word meanings.
numbers: Exp 1: letters 163 overextensions vs 46 underextensions; faces 239 vs 51. Participants: faces 34 made more overextensions than underextensions, 8 the reverse (sign test z=3.86, p<.001). Overextension by dimension: letter shape 37%, colour 12%; intelligence 51%, emotion 13%.
limits: Zero ratings excluded (5% letters, 20% faces); some inconsistency is noise; four experiments.
agent_relevance: The effect holds in perception, so it is a general property of how graded categories are combined, not only of words.

source: Hampton (1996) Conjunctions of visually based categories (Exp 3 and 4)
finding: The vaguer dimension gets overextended more. Making the vaguer dimension more important raises overextension.
numbers: Exp 3 augmented condition raised overextension of age from 30% to 41% and double overextension from 6% to 16%. Exp 4: age overextended 50% vs emotion 20%, with similar boundary sharpness (S=25% and 22%).
limits: Face stimuli show more than letters; asymmetric compensation between dimensions.
agent_relevance: Parent concepts do not weigh the same in a blend. The vaguer, more abstract parent gives way.

source: Hampton (1997) Conceptual combination: conjunction and negation of natural concepts
finding: Replicated overextension, concept dominance and non-commutativity for conjunctions such as Tools which are also Weapons. Negated conjunctions (Tools which are not Weapons) are also overextended. Membership in a conjunction follows a geometric average of constituent membership values.
numbers: Two experiments (abstract). Attribute generation for negated categories followed rated frequency in the negated category.
limits: Cell counts not extracted this session.
agent_relevance: A product (geometric mean) rule is a simple, code-computable merge score for two parents.

source: Hampton (1996) Conceptual combination chapter: Selective Modification Model (Smith, Osherson, Rips & Keane 1988)
finding: A modifier moves all votes in one slot (colour) to one value and raises that slot's weight. It predicts brown apple is more typical of brown apple than of apple. Hampton calls it over-specified: moving the votes alone gives the same prediction.
numbers: Example frame: COLOUR = red 10, green 8, yellow 5, brown 2 votes.
limits: Works for intersective adjectives (brown apple); not for noun-noun relations.
agent_relevance: A slot-and-filler frame per concept is easy to hold in a prompt or table: swap one slot value, keep the rest.

source: Hampton (1996) chapter on Murphy (1988) and extensional feedback
finding: Murphy (1988) showed emergent properties in combinations (casual shirts are pulled over the head though casual things and shirts are not). Hampton and Rips argue these come from peeking at known instances (No Peeking Principle), not from computing from the parts.
numbers: Examples: boiled eggs hard vs boiled potatoes soft; stop signs hexagonal. Adjectives like open take many meanings by noun (open year, open hand).
limits: Conceptual debate; no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Separate in the agent: properties recalled for a known combination vs properties built for a novel one.

source: Hampton (1996) chapter on Wisniewski (1996): construal and property mapping
finding: Novel noun-noun combinations are not always read as a relation (slot filling, mountain magazine). Often a salient property of the modifier is mapped onto the head (tiger hound = hound with stripes). Two more routes: hybrid (horse cow) and construal of a noun as a part or related thing (tiger chair = chair covered in tiger skin).
numbers: Wisniewski paired nouns from animals, artifacts, substances (no substance-substance). Property mapping was most frequent for animal-animal. Davidson and Stevenson (1995): natural-kind pairs gave more property mapping than artifact pairs.
limits: Second-hand through Hampton's chapter.
agent_relevance: Four interpretation moves for the agent: relation link, property map, hybrid, construal. Pick by how similar the two concepts are.

source: Bock & Clifton (2000) The role of salience in conceptual combination (earlier studies they cite)
finding: Similar concepts promote property mapping (Wisniewski 1996). A salient modifier feature that matches a key head dimension drives property mapping (Estes and Glucksberg 2000).
numbers: Wisniewski 1996 Exp 2: 72% property mapping (high similarity) vs 48% (low similarity). Estes and Glucksberg: 79% for H-H (salient modifier feature relevant to head), 23% for H-L, 16% for L-H.
limits: Quoted through Bock and Clifton, originals not read. Wisniewski's similarity manipulation was extreme (sister terms vs distinct categories).
agent_relevance: Pick seeds where one concept has one very salient feature and the other has a matching dimension.

source: Bock & Clifton (2000) The role of salience in conceptual combination (own experiment)
finding: Highly salient features drove property-mapping readings. Natural kinds gave more property mapping than artifacts. Assessed similarity did not predict property mapping once pairs were randomly paired within ontological category.
numbers: 160 novel noun-noun pairs: 20 in each of 8 groups (high/low salience of N1 and N2 x artifacts/natural kinds), four lists of 40. Mean similarity 2.64 on 1-7, no group difference, F(7,150)=1.16, p>.30. Similarity vs property mapping r=-.06 overall, -.08 natural kinds, -.22 artifacts.
limits: Very similar pairs (zebra horse) and lexicalized pairs removed, so the similarity range is limited. Failed to reproduce a strong similarity effect.
agent_relevance: A seed pair needs a salient feature, not just closeness.

source: Gagne & Shoben (1997) CARIN theory, as described in Maguire et al. (2007)
finding: People read a noun-noun compound by choosing a relation (one of 16, e.g. LOCATED, DURING, FOR) from a competing pool. Availability depends on how often the modifier has gone with that relation, not the head.
numbers: Gagne and Shoben reported r=.44 between their relation-strength formula and response time, higher than raw relation frequency (r=-.34).
limits: Original not opened; quoted through the 2007 reanalysis.
agent_relevance: A short relation vocabulary (about 16 types), ranked by modifier, gives the agent candidate meanings.

source: Maguire, Devereux, Costello & Cater (2007) A reanalysis of the CARIN theory of conceptual combination
finding: Failed to support competition between relations. The CARIN formula's advantage comes from a free parameter. The original relation frequencies are not representative of the British National Corpus.
numbers: Removing the free parameter dropped r from .44 to .34, no better than the top relation's probability alone. Response time vs distance to nearest competing relation: r=-.09 (p=.66, N=28) with original frequencies and r=.08 (p=.70, N=26) with corpus frequencies. Close vs distant competitor groups: 1,030 ms (SD 94) vs 1,073 ms (SD 75).
limits: Commentary reanalysis, no new human data.
agent_relevance: Main-relation frequency matters; there is no good evidence for a competition process. Do not build a competing-relations vote.

source: Gagne & Shoben (2002) Priming relations in ambiguous noun-noun combinations
finding: A prime with the same relation speeds interpretation of an ambiguous combination (adolescent doctor after adolescent magazine). Results contradict schema-based theories and need changes to relation-based ones.
numbers: Exp 1: target responses 224 ms faster after a dominant-relation prime and 143 ms faster after a subdominant-relation prime than after unrelated primes. Exp 2: 37 participants in one version.
limits: Definition-verification RT; Exp 2 uses sentence exposure.
agent_relevance: Earlier context steers which relation gets picked. Keep context clean per combination, or vary primes on purpose.

source: Aerts & Sozzo (2014) Modeling concept combinations in a quantum-theoretic framework
finding: Hampton's membership data on conjunctions cannot fit one classical (Kolmogorov) probability space. A quantum model in Fock space, with interference and emergence, fits them.
numbers: Mint: food 0.87, plant 0.81, food-and-plant 0.90, so double overextension; excess over the minimum 0.09. Classical model needs mu(A and B) <= min(mu(A), mu(B)) and 0 <= 1 - mu(A) - mu(B) + mu(A and B).
limits: Hampton's reply: his 1988 data had about 10 participants per item, too few for complex fits.
agent_relevance: A curve fit, not a mechanism. Treat as description.

source: Hampton (2013/2014) Conceptual combination: extension and intension (commentary on Aerts, Gabora & Sozzo)
finding: Typicality and graded membership are not the same variable. The composite prototype model already explains the data qualitatively. Concepts are built afresh in context, so intensions (property sets), not extensions, combine.
numbers: Quantum data from Hampton 1988b used about 10 participants per item. The guppy effect concerns typicality (Smith et al. 1988); overextension concerns categorisation (Hampton 1988b).
limits: Commentary, theory level.
agent_relevance: Context decides which properties of each parent show. The agent should write the context for each merge.

source: Aerts et al. (2016) Context and interference effects in the combinations of natural concepts
finding: Quantum framework with context and interference for conjunctions and disjunctions. An item acts as a context that changes the state of the concept. Unified account of overextension and underextension.
numbers: Hampton's 7-point scale (+3 to -3) turned into normalized membership weights; Mint: 0.87 food, 0.81 plant, 0.9 both. Also Fruits or Vegetables disjunction (underextension).
limits: Fits published data; no new participants in the sections read.
agent_relevance: Same parent concept looks different in different contexts.

source: Costello & Keane (2000) Efficient creativity: constraint-guided conceptual combination (C3 model)
finding: Three pragmatic constraints guide combination: diagnosticity, plausibility, informativeness. The C3 model interprets compound phrases with results said to agree with people. Creativity arises because the constraints can be met in many ways.
numbers: No numbers: only a search-result summary was seen; Cognitive Science 24, 299-349 could not be opened.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Three tests for any candidate blend: does it distinguish the head, is it plausible, does it add information.

source: Wisniewski (1997) When concepts combine
finding: Computational-level account of combination plus an algorithmic account that stresses comparison and construction. Also links noun-noun combination to nominal metaphor.
numbers: Not opened (Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 4, 167-183); abstract-level summary only.
limits: Full text did not load.
agent_relevance: Compare the two concepts first (align shared structure), then construct what is needed.

source: Li, Carlson & Potts (2022) Systematicity in GPT-3's interpretation of novel English noun compounds (Exp 1 and 3)
finding: GPT-3 matched human meaning-type distributions (Levin et al. 2019) for novel compounds. But with nonsense words defined only in context the match vanished, which points to memory of real words, not abstract artifact vs natural-kind reasoning.
numbers: Exp 1: 38 compounds x 3 prompts x 4 temperatures = 456 generations, Fleiss kappa .844 (meta-relations). Correlation with humans up to 0.93 (few-shot, T=0.7). Exclusion rate 0 to 37% vs human 17.67%. Exp 3 (nonsense words): correlation with the human pattern only 0.105; about 30% of exclusions were head/modifier inversions.
limits: GPT-3 only; coded by the authors; small compound sets.
agent_relevance: LLMs look human on familiar patterns but not under abstract in-context rules. Test blend operators with nonce words.

source: Li, Carlson & Potts (2022), human reference distribution from Levin et al. (2019)
finding: Meaning type depends on the ontological type of the parents. Artifact-artifact gives event readings; natural-natural gives mostly environmental readings.
numbers: Event / perceptual / environmental %: artifact-artifact 93/7/0 (N=195); natural-artifact 88/12/0 (N=157); artifact-natural 66/34/0 (N=157); natural-natural 15/34/51 (N=148).
limits: Human data quoted from Levin et al. 2019, not read in the original.
agent_relevance: Ontological type of the two parents predicts which link to try first.

source: Song et al. (2025) Is a peeled apple still red? LLMs and conceptual combination with property type (CCPT)
finding: 12,315 triples of noun phrase, property and type (inherited, emergent, canceled). LLMs find emergent properties harder to produce than canceled ones, and writing a noun phrase that shows a given emergent property is harder than naming the property.
numbers: GPT-4o: judging whether a phrase has a property 82.6% (95.6% when yes, 69.6% when no); naming the property type 56.4% vs human 81%. Emergence scores in noun-phrase completion 27 or lower for every model. Human check N=30 sampled items; LLM judge vs human on 300 pairs.
limits: LLM-as-judge scoring; ConceptNet-based gold labels.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the agent is weak at emergence. Needs an explicit step for it.

source: Song et al. (2025) CCPT: spread-activation prompting
finding: An iterative spread-activation prompt (activate related concepts from the LLM or ConceptNet, filter, repeat) beat base and chain-of-thought prompts on emergent properties. More iterations helped; dropping the filter step hurt.
numbers: Exact cell values in the PDF table were garbled in text extraction; the paper reports best scores for spread activation and gold emergence scores up to about 57 vs base GPT-4o lower.
limits: Table values not reliably read; treat as qualitative.
agent_relevance: Operator idea: spread to neighbours, filter, then merge.

source: Aerts et al. (2026) Identifying quantum structure in AI language (Bell tests with ChatGPT and Gemini)
finding: ChatGPT and Gemini violate a Bell (CHSH) inequality on a combined concept (The Animal Acts: tiger/cat, snorts/meows), as human groups did.
numbers: Human-type reference CHSH=2.4197 (classical limit 2, quantum bound 2.83). ChatGPT (81 trials) prompt 1: 2.25; prompt 2: 3.09, above the quantum bound; mean 2.67. Gemini prompt 1: 2.12; prompt 2: 4 (maximal); mean 3.06.
limits: Interpretive claim; values above 2.83 mean it is not a simple quantum model; no classical-simulator control.
agent_relevance: Shows LLMs reproduce the non-classical pattern of human combination. It says nothing about blend quality.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Do vision-language models understand compound nouns? (Compun)
finding: CLIP-type models do worse on compound nouns than on their parts. A prompt with an LLM-written caption improves retrieval.
numbers: Compun benchmark: 400 unique compound nouns. The caption method improves CLIP by 8.25% and OpenCLIP by 2.35%.
limits: Retrieval, not generation.
agent_relevance: An explicit written gloss of a compound helps; a gloss step can come before any use of a blend.
